question: Which TWO scenarios are good fits for batch inference rather than real-time inference? (Select TWO.)
options: Scoring every customer for churn risk once a night
Suggesting the next word as a user types in a chat box
Generating product recommendations for all users before a weekly email campaign
Detecting fraud on a login attempt before the session starts
Approving a card payment while the customer waits at checkout
explanations: No one waits for each result, and the whole dataset is processed on a schedule.
Interactive suggestions need immediate responses.
Results are needed in bulk ahead of time, so batch processing is efficient.
The login flow waits for the decision, so it needs real-time inference.
A user is waiting, so this needs real-time inference.
takeaway: Nobody waiting + large volume → batch. Someone waiting → real-time.

question: Put these steps of an ML project that predicts customer churn in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.
options: Train and tune the model, then evaluate it on held-out data
Prepare the data and engineer features
Collect and label historical customer data
Deploy the model and monitor it in production
Define the business goal and how success will be measured
explanations: Training uses the prepared features, and evaluation on unseen data comes before deployment.
Data is cleaned and transformed into features before training.
Labeled historical data (who churned) is gathered once the goal is clear.
Only an evaluated model is deployed, and monitoring continues afterward.
Every ML project starts by framing the business problem and success metrics.
takeaway: Frame → collect → prepare → train and evaluate → deploy and monitor.

question: SageMaker Model Monitor reports that a deployed model's input data has drifted. Put the MLOps response steps in the correct order.
options: Retrain the model on the updated dataset
Approve and deploy the better model
Investigate the alert and confirm how the input data has changed
Evaluate the new model against the production model
Collect recent, representative labeled data
explanations: Training on current data addresses the drift.
Deployment happens only after the evaluation gate.
Confirm the drift and understand it before acting.
The new model must beat the current one before replacing it.
Retraining needs data that reflects the current population.
takeaway: Detect → investigate → collect current data → retrain → evaluate → deploy.

question: A team is preparing data for a supervised image classifier. Put these steps in the correct order.
options: Train the model on the training set and tune it on the validation set
Gather images that represent every class and condition
Split the labeled data into training, validation, and test sets
Label the images with the correct class using SageMaker Ground Truth
explanations: The test set stays untouched until the end.
Representative raw data comes first.
Splitting happens once labels exist, before any training.
Labels are added to the collected images.
takeaway: Collect → label → split → train and tune (test set held out).

question: Match each business problem with the ML technique that fits it. Each technique is used once.
prompts: Predict next month's revenue in dollars
Decide whether a loan applicant will default (yes or no)
Group customers into segments without predefined labels
Flag unusual sensor readings that don't match normal behavior
options: Binary classification
Clustering
Regression
Anomaly detection
explanations: The target is a continuous number, so this is regression.
There are two possible classes, so this is binary classification.
Finding groups in unlabeled data is clustering.
Identifying outliers compared with normal patterns is anomaly detection.
takeaway: Number → regression. Category → classification. Groups → clustering. Outliers → anomaly detection.

question: Match each scenario with the type of machine learning it describes. Each type is used at least once.
prompts: A model learns from emails already marked as spam or not spam
A robot learns to walk by receiving rewards for staying upright
An algorithm groups news articles by similarity without labels
A model predicts house prices from past sales with known prices
options: Reinforcement learning
Unsupervised learning
Supervised learning
explanations: Labeled examples with known outcomes mean supervised learning.
Learning actions from rewards in an environment is reinforcement learning.
Finding structure in unlabeled data is unsupervised learning.
Past sales with known prices are labeled examples, so this is supervised.
takeaway: Labels → supervised. No labels → unsupervised. Rewards → reinforcement.

question: Match each requirement with the AWS AI service that meets it. Each service is used once.
prompts: Extract text and tables from scanned forms
Detect objects and unsafe content in photos
Convert recorded meetings into text
Find sentiment and key phrases in customer reviews
Read product descriptions aloud
options: Amazon Textract
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Polly
explanations: Textract reads documents, including forms and tables.
Rekognition analyzes images and video.
Transcribe performs speech-to-text.
Comprehend is the managed NLP service for text insights.
Polly converts text to speech.
takeaway: Documents → Textract. Images → Rekognition. Speech → text: Transcribe. Text insights → Comprehend. Text → speech: Polly.

question: In the context of large language models, what is a token?
options: A unit of text such as a word, part of a word, or punctuation mark
A security credential that authorizes each call to the model API
A labeled training example used when fine-tuning the model
A single complete sentence, which is the unit used for pricing
explanations: Models read and generate text as tokens, and pricing and limits are counted in tokens.
That describes an access token for authentication, not an LLM token.
Training examples contain many tokens; they are not tokens themselves.
A sentence usually contains many tokens.
takeaway: Tokens are sub-word units; models are priced and limited by token counts.

question: What is an embedding in generative AI applications?
options: An encryption key that protects model inputs
A compressed copy of a document used for backup and recovery
A numeric vector that represents the meaning of data
A prompt template with variables for user input
explanations: Encryption keys are unrelated to embeddings.
Embeddings are not backups; they represent meaning.
Items with similar meaning have embeddings that are close together, which enables semantic search.
Templates are reusable prompts, not numeric representations.
takeaway: Embedding = vector that captures meaning → used for semantic search and RAG.

question: What is the main purpose of a vector database in a RAG application?
options: To store the foundation model's weights close to the application
To translate documents into multiple languages
To store embeddings and find the ones most similar to a query
To record every prompt and response for auditing
explanations: Model weights are hosted by the model service, not by a vector database.
Translation is done by services such as Amazon Translate.
Vector databases index embeddings for fast similarity (nearest-neighbor) search.
Prompt audit logs belong in logging services such as invocation logging.
takeaway: Vector database = store and search embeddings by similarity.

question: Why do RAG applications split long documents into chunks before creating embeddings?
options: To encrypt each part of the document separately with its own key
So retrieval returns focused passages that fit in the model's context
To reduce the number of tokens billed by the embeddings model
To reduce the storage cost of the original documents in Amazon S3
explanations: Chunking is not an encryption technique.
Smaller passages match questions more precisely and keep the prompt within the context window.
The same text (plus any overlap) is still embedded, so chunking doesn't cut embedding cost.
The original documents are usually kept; chunking isn't about storage.
takeaway: Chunking makes retrieval precise and context-sized.

question: What makes a foundation model multimodal?
options: It is offered by several model providers through one API.
It handles more than one data type, such as text and images.
It is available in several AWS Regions at the same time.
It can be fine-tuned with several datasets of different sizes.
explanations: Model providers are unrelated to modality.
Multimodal models handle multiple data types, for example image and text input with text output.
Regional availability is unrelated to modality.
Fine-tuning ability isn't what makes a model multimodal.
takeaway: Multimodal = more than one data type in or out.

question: Which characteristic distinguishes a foundation model from a traditional, task-specific ML model?
options: It is trained on labeled data for a single, well-defined task.
It produces explainable predictions from a small set of features.
It is pre-trained on broad data and adapts to many tasks.
It is trained mainly on one company's private data.
explanations: That describes a traditional, task-specific model, the opposite of an FM.
That describes an interpretable traditional model, not an FM.
FMs learn general capabilities from large, diverse data, so one model can summarize, answer questions, translate, and more.
FMs are typically pre-trained on broad public data; private data is added later with RAG or fine-tuning.
takeaway: FM = large, pre-trained on broad data, adaptable to many tasks.

question: A generative AI assistant cites a research paper that does not exist. What is this called?
options: Prompt leaking
Overfitting
Data drift
Hallucination
explanations: Prompt leaking exposes a system prompt. Nothing confidential was revealed here.
Overfitting is a training problem where a model memorizes its training data.
Data drift describes changes in input data over time.
The model generated plausible-sounding but false information.
takeaway: Confident but false output → hallucination.

question: A company asks a foundation model about its new pricing plan, which was published yesterday. The model answers with last year's prices. Which approach will MOST directly give the model the current information?
options: Retrieve the current pricing document and add it to the prompt
Increase the model's temperature so it considers newer answers
Switch to a larger model with more parameters and knowledge
Lower the maximum output tokens to prevent outdated details
explanations: RAG supplies up-to-date facts at inference time, so the model answers from the current document.
Temperature changes randomness, not what the model knows.
A bigger model still doesn't know about yesterday's pricing.
Output length has nothing to do with the model's knowledge.
takeaway: Recent or private facts → supply them at inference time with RAG or tools.

question: Why can the same prompt return different answers from a generative model on different requests?
options: Because AWS routes each request to a different model family
Because the model samples each next token from probabilities
Because the prompt is encrypted differently each time
Because the model is retrained after every request
explanations: The same model is used; variation comes from sampling.
Sampling introduces randomness; lower temperature and top-p reduce it.
Encryption in transit doesn't change the output.
Models are not retrained between requests.
takeaway: Sampling makes outputs nondeterministic.

question: Which use case is the BEST fit for generative AI?
options: Predicting next week's inventory levels from sales history
Generating unit tests and documentation from existing source code
Detecting fraudulent card transactions in milliseconds
Calculating payroll taxes from fixed legal formulas
explanations: This is time-series forecasting, a traditional ML task.
Code generation and documentation are strong generative AI use cases.
Low-latency fraud scoring on structured data suits traditional ML.
Exact, rule-based calculations belong in conventional code.
takeaway: GenAI creates content (text, code, images); prediction on structured data is traditional ML.

question: A company wants to cut the on-demand cost of a Bedrock application. Responses average 1,500 tokens, but users only read the first paragraph. Which change reduces cost MOST directly?
options: Increase the temperature so answers end sooner
Add more few-shot examples of short answers to the prompt
Ask for shorter responses and lower the maximum output tokens
Switch to a model with a larger context window
explanations: Temperature doesn't change response length or price.
Examples increase input tokens and cost.
Fewer output tokens directly reduce cost, and output tokens are usually priced higher than input tokens.
A larger context window doesn't make responses shorter and may cost more.
takeaway: Cut unused output → shorter responses + max output tokens.

question: Which Amazon Bedrock option lets a company purchase dedicated model capacity for predictable, high-volume production traffic?
options: Intelligent Prompt Routing
Batch inference
Prompt caching
Provisioned Throughput
explanations: Prompt routing picks between models per request; it doesn't reserve capacity.
Batch inference processes offline jobs asynchronously; it doesn't reserve capacity.
Prompt caching lowers the cost of repeated prompt prefixes.
Provisioned Throughput purchases model units that provide dedicated throughput, billed hourly.
takeaway: Dedicated, predictable capacity → Provisioned Throughput.

question: A company needs to classify 2 million support tickets from last year with an FM on Amazon Bedrock. Results are needed within a week. Which approach is the MOST cost-effective?
options: Use the Priority service tier for every request
Submit a Bedrock batch inference job with the tickets in Amazon S3
Call the model on demand from a script, one ticket at a time
Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment
explanations: Priority costs more; this job isn't urgent.
Batch inference runs asynchronously over S3 data at a discount to on-demand for supported models.
This pays full on-demand prices and is likely to be throttled.
A long commitment for a one-off job is wasteful.
takeaway: Large, non-urgent job → Bedrock batch inference.

question: A company runs two Amazon Bedrock workloads on the same model: a customer chat that must respond as fast as possible at peak times, and nightly document summarization that can wait. Which service tier choice BEST balances cost and performance?
options: Priority tier for the chat and Flex tier for the summarization
Standard tier for the chat and Priority tier for the summarization
Priority tier for both workloads
Flex tier for the chat and Priority tier for the summarization
explanations: Priority gives the fastest responses for a premium; Flex is discounted for workloads that tolerate longer processing.
The latency-sensitive workload should get priority, not the nightly job.
Paying the Priority premium for work that can wait wastes money.
This is reversed: Flex is for work that can wait.
takeaway: Latency-critical → Priority. Can wait → Flex (discounted).

question: Many requests to a Bedrock model start with the same 5,000-token product manual, followed by a short, different question. Which feature reduces cost and latency for this pattern?
options: Batch inference
Model distillation
Prompt caching
Cross-Region inference
explanations: Batch is for offline jobs; these are interactive questions.
Distillation creates a smaller model; it doesn't address the repeated prefix.
Caching the repeated prefix avoids reprocessing it on every request, lowering cost and time to first token.
Cross-Region inference spreads load; it doesn't avoid reprocessing the manual.
takeaway: Repeated long prefix → prompt caching.

question: A company wants Amazon Bedrock to send simple questions to a smaller model and complex questions to a larger model in the same family automatically. Which feature should it use?
options: Provisioned Throughput
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
Model distillation
Intelligent Prompt Routing
explanations: Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for one model.
Guardrails filter content; they don't choose models.
Distillation trains a smaller model; it doesn't route individual requests.
Prompt routing predicts which model in a family can answer each request well and routes it to the most cost-effective one.
takeaway: Per-request choice between a small and large model → Intelligent Prompt Routing.

question: Which Amazon Bedrock capability helps absorb traffic spikes by routing on-demand requests across multiple AWS Regions?
options: Amazon CloudFront
Model invocation logging
Cross-Region inference profiles
Provisioned Throughput
explanations: CloudFront is a content delivery network, not a model routing feature.
Logging records requests; it doesn't add capacity.
Inference profiles distribute on-demand requests across Regions to increase available throughput.
Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity in one Region with a commitment.
takeaway: Bursty traffic, no residency limits → cross-Region inference.

question: A company self-hosts a deep learning model on Amazon EC2 and wants to lower the cost of serving predictions at high volume. Which AWS chip family is designed for cost-efficient inference?
options: AWS Graviton processors
AWS Inferentia
Amazon ElastiCache nodes
AWS Trainium
explanations: Graviton is a general-purpose Arm CPU family; it isn't designed as an ML inference accelerator.
Inferentia-based instances are built for high-performance, low-cost inference.
ElastiCache is an in-memory cache, not an ML accelerator.
Trainium is designed for cost-efficient training.
takeaway: Training → Trainium. Inference → Inferentia.

question: A team wants an email alert when its monthly Amazon Bedrock spending is forecast to exceed $2,000. Which AWS service should it use?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Budgets
AWS CloudTrail
explanations: Trusted Advisor gives best-practice recommendations, not budget alerts.
Cost Explorer analyzes and visualizes spending; budget alerts are set in AWS Budgets.
Budgets tracks cost against a limit and alerts when actual or forecast spend exceeds it.
CloudTrail records API calls, not spending.
takeaway: Alert on spend thresholds → AWS Budgets. Analyze spend → Cost Explorer.

question: A legal team wants to send entire 300-page contracts to a model in one request for analysis. Which model characteristic should it check FIRST?
options: Whether the model can generate images
The model's default temperature
The maximum context window size
The number of languages the model supports
explanations: Image generation is irrelevant to contract analysis.
Temperature controls randomness, not input size.
The whole contract plus instructions and output must fit within the context window.
Language support matters but doesn't decide whether the contract fits.
takeaway: Long inputs in one request → check the context window.

question: A company with no ML expertise wants to add a text-summarization feature by calling a pre-trained foundation model through an API, with no servers to manage. Which AWS service fits BEST?
options: Amazon Comprehend custom classification
Amazon EC2 with GPU instances
Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs
Amazon Bedrock
explanations: Custom classification labels text; it doesn't generate summaries with an FM.
Self-hosting means managing servers and model serving.
Training jobs are for building your own models and require ML skills.
Bedrock provides serverless API access to foundation models from multiple providers.
takeaway: Serverless FM access, no ML expertise → Bedrock.

question: A research team wants to try several publicly available foundation models, deploy one to a SageMaker endpoint inside its VPC, and fine-tune it later with its own scripts. Where should the team start?
options: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
Amazon Q Developer
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon Quick
explanations: Prompt Management stores and versions prompts; it doesn't deploy models.
Q Developer is a coding assistant, not a model hub.
JumpStart is a hub of pre-trained and open models that deploy to SageMaker endpoints you control and support fine-tuning.
Quick is a ready-made assistant for business users.
takeaway: Open models you deploy and control → SageMaker JumpStart.

question: A sales operations team wants a ready-made AI assistant that answers questions about company dashboards and documents and automates weekly reporting tasks, without any development work. Which AWS offering fits BEST?
options: AWS Transform
Amazon Bedrock Agents
Amazon Quick
Amazon SageMaker Canvas
explanations: Transform modernizes legacy applications.
Bedrock Agents are for developers who build their own agent applications.
Quick gives business users AI agents, research, BI dashboards, and workflow automation over their data without building an app.
Canvas builds predictive ML models without code; it isn't a BI and automation assistant.
takeaway: Business users, no development, dashboards + automation → Amazon Quick.

question: Which AWS offering is an agentic IDE that turns a prompt into a spec with requirements, design, and tasks before generating code?
options: Amazon Bedrock Flows
Kiro
Amazon SageMaker Studio
AWS Transform
explanations: Flows orchestrates generative AI workflows; it isn't an IDE.
Kiro provides spec-driven development: requirements, design, and a task list before code.
Studio is an ML development environment, not a spec-driven coding IDE.
Transform modernizes legacy workloads.
takeaway: Spec-driven agentic IDE → Kiro.

question: A developer wants to write an agent in a few lines of Python using an open-source framework, connect it to MCP tools, and later host it on AWS. Which option fits BEST for writing the agent?

Strands Agents

AWS Transform
explanations: Kiro assists general software development.

question: A company wants the lowest-latency, lowest-cost Amazon Nova model for a text-only classification task. Which model should it evaluate first?

question: Which is an advantage of building generative AI applications with managed AWS services such as Amazon Bedrock instead of training and hosting your own model?

Costs are fixed each month regardless of usage.
The company no longer needs to secure its own data or access.

question: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP) used for?

Connecting agents to tools and data sources in a standard way
Measuring the quality of model and agent responses
Compressing long prompts to reduce token costs

MCP is an open standard for how agents discover and call tools and access data.
Evaluation uses metrics and judges, not MCP.
MCP doesn't compress prompts.

question: An AI assistant must tell customers the real-time status of their orders. Which design lets it provide accurate, current answers?

Give the agent a tool that calls the order-tracking API
Ask the model to estimate the delivery date
Increase the model's context window

A tool retrieves live data from the source system, so answers reflect the real status.
Estimates without data are guesses and can be wrong.
A larger window doesn't give access to live data.
takeaway: Live data or real actions → tools.

question: A personal-finance assistant should remember a user's risk preference in future conversations weeks later. Which capability is MOST appropriate?

Fine-tuning a separate model for each user
Lowering the temperature so answers stay consistent
Long-term memory (for example, AgentCore Memory)

Per-user fine-tuning is impractical and costly.
Temperature controls randomness, not memory.
Long-term memory stores extracted facts and preferences so they can be recalled across sessions.

question: An agent that helps with IT troubleshooting gets confused because its prompts contain dozens of irrelevant tool outputs from earlier steps. Which practice BEST addresses this?

Summarize or drop stale tool outputs and keep only what each step needs
Add more few-shot examples showing how to ignore irrelevant output
Switch to a model with a larger context window so all outputs still fit
explanations: Output length doesn't fix a cluttered input.
Context engineering curates what goes into each call, which improves focus, cost, and latency.
Examples add tokens; they don't remove irrelevant content.
More room lets even more irrelevant content in.
takeaway: Curate context per step — relevance beats volume.

question: Which situation is the BEST fit for an autonomous AI agent rather than a fixed workflow?
options: A nightly job converts the day's files from CSV to Parquet format
A research assistant picks its sources and tools based on each question
A payroll system applies fixed tax rules to each employee
Invoices follow the same four approved steps each time, for auditors
explanations: This is a fixed data-processing task with no decisions to make.
When the path depends on the request, an agent can plan and choose tools dynamically.
Exact rules belong in deterministic code.
A fixed, auditable sequence suits a deterministic workflow.

question: An online retailer launches a generative AI shopping assistant. Which metric BEST shows whether the assistant increases revenue per customer?

Model latency at the 99th percentile during peak shopping hours
Average number of tokens per conversation with the assistant
Average revenue per user (ARPU) versus customers without the assistant

Latency is an operational metric.
Token counts relate to cost, not revenue.
ARPU against a control group shows whether the assistant raises revenue per customer.

question: Why is it difficult to use an LLM for decisions that regulators require to be fully explained?
options: LLMs refuse to answer financial questions because of built-in safety filters.
LLMs cannot reliably process numeric inputs such as incomes and credit scores.
Their reasoning can't be traced, and self-explanations may not be faithful.
LLM outputs can't be logged, so decisions can't be stored for audit.
explanations: LLMs can answer finance questions.
LLMs can process numbers; that isn't the issue.
LLM decisions come from billions of parameters, so faithful explanations are hard to provide.
Model invocation logging can store prompts and responses; logging isn't the issue.
takeaway: Faithful explanations required → interpretable models, not LLM self-explanations.

question: A company is deciding whether to use generative AI to answer customer billing questions. Which TWO risks should it plan for? (Select TWO.)
options: Answers to the same question may vary between requests.
The model will store each customer's billing data in its weights.
The model may give confident but incorrect answers.
The model will automatically know each customer's current bill.
The company must manage its own GPU cluster to serve answers.
explanations: Nondeterminism can produce inconsistent answers.
Inference doesn't change model weights; prompts aren't learned by the model.
Hallucinations are a key risk for customer-facing answers.
Private, current data must be supplied through RAG or tools.
Managed services such as Amazon Bedrock need no GPU management.
takeaway: Plan for hallucination, nondeterminism, and missing private data.

question: A company's Bedrock application sends a long, unchanging system prompt with every request and returns long answers. Traffic is interactive and varies during the day. Which TWO actions will MOST reduce cost? (Select TWO.)
options: Enable prompt caching for the repeated system prompt
Move all requests to batch inference
Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a long commitment
Ask for concise answers and set a lower maximum output token limit
Increase the temperature to shorten answers
explanations: Caching avoids reprocessing the unchanged prefix on each request.
Batch inference is asynchronous and can't serve interactive users.
Variable traffic makes a long commitment inefficient.
Output tokens are usually the most expensive tokens.
Temperature doesn't control length or cost.
takeaway: Repeated prefix → caching. Long answers → cap output. Variable traffic → avoid long commitments.

question: Which TWO components are typically part of an AI agent built with Amazon Bedrock? (Select TWO.)
options: A fine-tuned model, which every Bedrock agent requires before it can run
Action groups that define the APIs the agent can call
A dedicated Amazon Redshift cluster
A GPU cluster that the customer provisions and manages for the agent
A foundation model that reasons about which step to take next

Redshift isn't a required agent component.
Bedrock is serverless; customers don't manage GPU clusters for agents.
The FM plans and decides which actions to take.

question: Put these stages of the foundation model lifecycle in the correct order.

Select and prepare the training data

Fine-tune the model for specific tasks
Deploy the model and collect feedback
explanations: Pre-training builds general capabilities from the selected data.
Data selection comes first.
Evaluation happens before deployment.

Feedback from production informs the next iteration.

question: An agent receives the request "Rebook my cancelled flight." Put the steps it typically follows in order.

Review the tool results and choose the best option
Interpret the goal and plan the steps
Call the booking tool to make the change
Call a tool to look up the booking and available flights
explanations: The agent reports the outcome.
It reasons over the results before acting.
The agent first works out what the user wants and how to achieve it.
The action is taken once a choice is made.
It gathers live information with tools.

question: Put the steps an LLM follows to generate a response in the correct order.
options: Append the token and repeat until a stop condition
Sample the next token using settings such as temperature
Calculate probabilities for the next token
Split the prompt into tokens
Process the tokens with self-attention layers
explanations: Generation continues until a stop sequence or the token limit.
Inference parameters control how the next token is chosen.
The model outputs a probability for each possible next token.
Text is first converted into tokens.
The transformer relates every token to the others.

question: Match each workload with the Amazon Bedrock option that fits it BEST. Each option is used once.
prompts: Unpredictable, low-volume internal assistant

question: Match each need with the AWS offering designed for it. Each offering is used once.
prompts: Developers call FMs from several providers through one API

question: Match each description with the type of model. Each type is used once.

question: A prompt includes three example questions with their ideal answers, followed by a new question. Which technique is this?

Chain-of-thought prompting
Few-shot prompting

Several worked examples in the prompt make this few-shot prompting.

Retraining a model on the latest company data every night so that it stays current
Compressing a large model into a smaller one that learns from its outputs

The model adapts its behavior from the context it is given at inference time.
Retraining changes weights; in-context learning doesn't.

Remove the examples so the model isn't distracted
Ask the model to reason step by step before answering

More randomness makes multi-step reasoning less reliable.

Chain-of-thought prompting encourages intermediate reasoning, which improves multi-step tasks.

Hallucination

Tell the model in the system prompt to keep other customers' data private
Switch to a model with a longer context window and stronger reasoning
Treat retrieved text as untrusted and enforce user permissions outside the model

Prompt instructions can be overridden and are not a reliable control.
Context length doesn't affect injection risk.
If the application only ever retrieves data the current user may see, injected instructions can't expose others' data.
takeaway: Injected instructions in documents → treat content as data and enforce authorization outside the model.

question: A public chatbot is being jailbroken with role-play prompts. Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails setting is designed to detect these attempts?

Contextual grounding check
Sensitive information filters
The prompt attack filter in content filters
explanations: Word lists are easy to bypass with different phrasing.

These detect PII, not jailbreak attempts.
The prompt attack filter detects jailbreaks and prompt injection attempts in user input.
takeaway: Jailbreak and injection attempts → Guardrails prompt attack filter.

question: A developer wants to cap each response at about 200 words to control cost. Which inference parameter should the developer set?

Maximum output tokens
Top-k
Top-p (nucleus sampling)

Top-p limits candidate tokens by cumulative probability, not length.

Responses become about 30% shorter because generation stops earlier.
The first 30% of the prompt is processed and the rest is skipped, which reduces input token cost.
The model runs 30% of its transformer layers, which makes responses faster.

Top-p doesn't control length.
The whole prompt is always processed.
Top-p doesn't change the model's architecture.
takeaway: Lower top-p → fewer candidate tokens → less randomness.

It retrieves relevant data and adds it to the prompt for the model to use.
It filters harmful or off-topic content out of the model's responses.

That describes distillation or quantization.
RAG grounds answers in retrieved data at query time.
That describes guardrails.
takeaway: RAG = retrieve relevant data → add to prompt → generate grounded answer.

question: A company adds 500 new policy documents to the Amazon S3 bucket used by its Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, but the assistant can't answer questions about them. What is the MOST likely fix?

Switch to a larger embeddings model
Increase the model's temperature
Run a sync (ingestion job) for the data source
explanations: Knowledge bases don't need fine-tuning; they need the new content indexed.
The documents haven't been ingested at all yet.
Temperature doesn't add knowledge.
Syncing chunks, embeds, and indexes the new documents so they can be retrieved.
takeaway: New documents invisible → sync the knowledge base data source.

Hierarchical chunking, which returns the parent section of each matching chunk
Fixed-size chunking with smaller chunks so that each match is more precise

Whole documents may exceed the context window and dilute relevance.
This keeps retrieval precise while giving the model fuller context.

takeaway: Precise matches + fuller context → hierarchical chunking.

Provisioned Throughput
Prompt caching
Word filters
explanations: A reranker re-scores retrieved chunks for relevance so the top few can be used.
Capacity doesn't improve relevance.
Caching reuses repeated prefixes; it doesn't rank chunks.
Word filters block specific words in content.
takeaway: Better ordering of retrieved chunks → reranking.

question: Users search a knowledge base for error codes such as "ERR-4471". Semantic search often misses exact codes. Which retrieval approach helps MOST?

Hybrid search that combines keyword and semantic search
Switch to a larger text generation model
Increase the embeddings model's vector dimensions

Keyword matching finds exact codes while semantic search handles meaning.
The generator can't fix what retrieval missed.
More dimensions don't guarantee exact-term matching.
takeaway: Exact codes, names, or rare terms → hybrid search.

question: An application needs to fetch relevant chunks from an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base and combine them with CRM data in its own custom prompt. Which API should it call?

RetrieveAndGenerate
Retrieve
explanations: ApplyGuardrail evaluates text against a guardrail.

question: A team wants a vector store for its Amazon Bedrock knowledge base without provisioning or managing search clusters. Which option fits BEST?

Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive

Amazon ElastiCache with Valkey
Amazon S3 Vectors

takeaway: Huge vector sets, infrequent queries, lowest cost → S3 Vectors.

question: Managers want to ask "What were total sales by region last quarter?" in plain English and get answers from data in Amazon Redshift. Which Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases capability fits?

A knowledge base for structured data that turns questions into SQL
Semantic search over the table and column descriptions
A denied topic that routes financial questions to analysts

Finding table descriptions doesn't compute totals.
Denied topics block topics; they don't answer queries.

question: An Amazon Bedrock agent must be able to create support tickets in the company's ticketing system. What must the developer configure?

An action group for the ticket API, backed by a Lambda function
A knowledge base containing the ticketing system manual
A higher maximum output token limit for longer ticket text

Action groups describe the operations an agent can call and connect them to your systems.
A knowledge base only retrieves information; it can't create tickets.
Output length doesn't let an agent call APIs.

question: A team wants to visually chain a prompt, a knowledge base lookup, a Lambda function, and a condition into a repeatable generative AI workflow. Which feature is designed for this?

question: A complex travel-planning task needs separate specialists for flights, hotels, and budgets, coordinated by one agent that combines their results. Which Amazon Bedrock capability supports this?

question: A company plans to fine-tune a model in Amazon Bedrock within a few months. What should it confirm when choosing the model now?

That the model has the largest context window among candidates

question: A company's product specifications change weekly, and the assistant must quote the latest values. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

Fine-tune the model every month
Continued pre-training on all historical specifications

RAG retrieves the latest documents at query time.
Monthly training leaves answers out of date between runs.
This is costly and still lags behind weekly changes.

question: A company needs an FM to always return a complex, company-specific report layout. Prompting and few-shot examples have been tried but are inconsistent. The company has 5,000 approved examples. Which approach should it try next?

Raise the temperature
Continued pre-training on public reports
Supervised fine-tuning on the approved examples
explanations: RAG supplies facts; the gap here is consistent learned behavior.
Higher temperature increases inconsistency.
Unlabeled public reports won't teach the company's layout.
Fine-tuning teaches consistent structure and style from many high-quality labeled examples.
takeaway: Consistent style/format with many labeled examples → fine-tuning.

Labeled prompt-response pairs
Images labeled with categories
Large amounts of unlabeled domain text
explanations: Preference rankings are used for RLHF.
Labeled pairs are used for supervised fine-tuning.
Labeled images are for image classifiers.
